newsitem.title: USA: Congress clears bill to lift U.S. tuna embargo.
newsitem.headline: Congress clears bill to lift U.S. tuna embargo.

text.p: The House of Representatives Thursday approved a compromise version of a bill to lift the U.S. embargo on tuna caught in nets that also may snare dolphins and sent the legislation to President Clinton.
The House unanimously agreed to changes the Senate made in the bill to move it to the White House before the Congress starts its month-long recess.

The legislation, sought by the White House at the urging of Mexico, would lift the embargo once a binding international agreement among Mexico, Venezuela and other nations is in effect to use measures that protect dolphins in the fishing process.

The United States imposed the embargo in 1994 after a public outcry over the slaughter of hundreds of thousands of dolphins that died in the huge encircling nets used to catch tuna in the Eastern Tropical Pacific Ocean.
Fishermen using helicopters and speed boats herded the dolphin and set nets on top of them, slashing and drowning dolphins to catch the tuna that tend to swim below in those waters.
To regain entry into the U.S. market, Mexico, Venezuela and about 10 other countries voluntarily adopted measures to free dolphin caught in the nets and minimise deaths.

The Clinton administration pushed repeal of the embargo as a way to encourage those countries to continue the safer fishing methods and to get them to join a legally binding agreement to protect dolphin.

But to see that dolphin are not harmed, the legislation would not allow cans of tuna caught in the encircling nets to be labeled as "dolphin safe" until March 1999 after a study on dolphin populations is done.
A number of Senate Democrats insisted that the definition of the label not be changed until there was proof that dolphin populations were not reduced once the embargo was lifted.
Major U.S. tuna companies adopted the "dolphin safe" label in 1990 to reassure consumers that they were not getting tuna at dolphins' expense, and the label later was put into law.
